structured.name: Tuvalu
structured._source: wikidata (CC0); landBorders + naturalResources from CIA World Factbook (public domain)

prose.hook: Tuvalu is one of the smallest and most remote countries on earth, a scattering of nine coral atolls in the South Pacific roughly halfway between Hawaii and Australia. It has no land borders with any country. Six of the atolls have lagoons open to the ocean, two have landlocked lagoons, and one has no lagoon at all, while fish and coconut form the resource base of daily life.
prose.physicalGeography: The country is made up of nine low-lying, narrow coral atolls scattered across the South Pacific Ocean, sitting about halfway between Hawaii and Australia. Six atolls -- Nanumea, Nui, Vaitupu, Nukufetau, Funafuti, and Nukulaelae -- have lagoons that open directly to the ocean. Nanumaya and Niutao instead have landlocked lagoons, and Niulakita has no lagoon at all.
prose.climate: The climate is tropical, moderated by easterly trade winds from March to November and marked by westerly gales and heavy rain from November to March. Severe tropical storms are usually rare, though 1997 brought three cyclones. Because the islands sit so low, they are highly sensitive to changes in sea level.
prose.economy: Tuvalu is classified as an upper middle-income Pacific island economy but is extremely environmentally fragile. Its currency is pegged to the Australian dollar, and it relies heavily on international aid alongside a subsistence agrarian sector, guided in part by the Te Kakeega sustainable development approach. Income also comes from licensing its internet domain name, while fishing remains the main industry and fish the leading export.
prose.peopleAndCulture: Tuvaluan and English are the official languages, alongside Samoan and, on the island of Nui, Kiribati. The population is overwhelmingly Protestant, at 92.7 percent, dominated by the Congregational Christian Church of Tuvalu at nearly 86 percent, with smaller Brethren, Seventh Day Adventist, Baha'i, and Jehovah's Witness communities. Ethnically the population is 97 percent Tuvaluan, with small shares of mixed Tuvaluan/I-Kiribati and Tuvaluan/other heritage.
